newsitem.title: UK: Amnesty urges Britain to protect human rights.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges Britain to protect human rights.

text.p: Amnesty International urged Britain's new Labour government on Friday to improve human rights on the British mainland and in Northern Ireland as a matter of priority.
The London-based human rights organisation said it had written to Prime Minister Tony Blair, elected by a landslide on May 1, with an agenda for human rights protection.
"The new government has an opportunity to make significant moves for human rights protection throughout the United Kingdom," Amnesty said in a statement.

"In our work on the country over the years, we have identified laws, procedures and practices of law enforcement officials which have led to violations of the rights to life, to freedom from torture or other forms of cruel treatment, to fair trial, and to freedom of expression and assembly."
Amnesty called on the government to bring Britain's laws into line with international standards and to set up a human rights commission.

The group called for an inquiry into what it said were significant numbers of deaths in police custody due to alleged violence, and into why a disproportionate number of the victims were from ethnic minorities.
Amnesty urged the re-instatement of the "historically recognised" right of suspects to remain silent during police interrogation and trial.
It also wanted the government to improve the human rights aspects of deportation and the political asylum process and to ensure that arms exports were formally tied to human rights considerations.

On Northern Ireland, gripped by sectarian and political conflict for nearly three decades, Amnesty said that because of the large number of human rights violations there it was essential to review policing and the emergency legislation brought in to combat extremist violence.
"The protection of human rights and the creation of a human rights culture are central to a lasting peace," Amnesty said.

It added: "Despite the many serious allegations of human rights violations in the past in Northern Ireland, there has been a marked failure by previous governments to carry out wide-ranging independent investigations into such allegations and make the findings public."

Amnesty also called for a review of the police in Northern Ireland, where the overwhelming number of officiers are Protestant, charged with overseeing conflict between their pro-British co-religionists and mainly Irish nationalist Catholics.
